questions.stem: Which definition matches the term pathogen?

options.text: An organism that brings about disease inside a different organism
options.explanation: This matches the note's definition.

options.text: Any microscopic particle found in the air
options.explanation: Pathogens are organisms causing disease, not any particle.

options.text: Any organism living inside a host
options.explanation: Many internal organisms are harmless; causing disease is the deciding property.

options.text: Any organism that feeds on dead material
options.explanation: Decomposer feeding is not disease-causing.

questions.stem: Which group of organisms includes pathogens but is NOT classified among living organisms?

options.text: Protoctists
options.explanation: Protoctists are living eukaryotes.

options.text: Viruses
options.explanation: Viruses cause disease yet sit outside the classification of living organisms.

options.text: Bacteria
options.explanation: Bacteria are living prokaryotes.

options.text: Fungi
options.explanation: Fungi are living eukaryotes.

questions.stem: How do pathogenic bacteria such as Pneumococcus sometimes behave, according to the note?

options.text: They only infect plants
options.explanation: Pneumonia is a human disease.

options.text: They are always harmless
options.explanation: They cause pneumonia.

options.text: They can stay within body cavities or spaces without infecting host cells
options.explanation: The note states they do not always infect host cells.

options.text: They always invade and take over host cells
options.explanation: That describes viruses, not these bacteria.

questions.stem: Which pairing of pathogen example and disease is correct?

options.text: Pneumococcus — malaria
options.explanation: Pneumococcus causes pneumonia.

options.text: Mucor — malaria in humans
options.explanation: Mucor is a plant-infecting fungus.

options.text: TMV — malaria
options.explanation: TMV is a plant virus.

options.text: Plasmodium falciparum — malaria spread by mosquitoes
options.explanation: The named protoctist and its vector pair correctly.

questions.stem: Why is 'all fungi are pathogens' a wrong claim to write in an exam?

options.text: Because only some Mucor species are pathogenic and most fungi are harmless decomposers or food makers
options.explanation: The note deliberately says some (but not all) Mucor species are pathogenic.

options.text: Because fungi are prokaryotes and cannot infect anything
options.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotes and some do infect.

options.text: Because fungi lack cell walls
options.explanation: Fungi have walls.

options.text: Because pathogens must be single-celled
options.explanation: Multicellular fungi can be pathogenic.

questions.stem: Give the term for an organism that brings about disease in a different organism.
Name the protoctist pathogen and the disease it causes.
Explain why the three named cellular pathogen groups can look so different from one another yet still share the pathogen label.
questions.modelAnswer: The label describes what an organism does — causing disease in a host — not how it is built, so a wall-carrying bacterium, a hyphal fungus and a parasite protoctist can all qualify despite sitting in three different classification groups.

questions.stem: A gardener finds a plant with discoloured, wilting leaves and suspects three culprits: a bacterium, a fungus and a virus. Using this note's examples, name one named species for two of the culprit classes.
questions.modelAnswer: A fungal culprit could be a Mucor species (some are plant pathogens) and a viral culprit could be tobacco mosaic virus; the bacterium slot would need a plant-infecting bacterial species rather than the human-lung Pneumococcus.

questions.stem: What does a virus particle contain?

options.text: Many types of nucleic acid and a nucleus
options.explanation: One nucleic acid type and no nucleus.

options.text: A protein coat around one type of nucleic acid
options.explanation: This matches the note's structure description.

options.text: A cell wall, membrane and cytoplasm
options.explanation: Viruses have no cellular structure.

options.text: Mitochondria and ribosomes
options.explanation: Viruses carry no organelles.

questions.stem: Why are viruses excluded from the classification of living organisms?

options.text: Because they cannot cause disease
options.explanation: Causing disease is what they do best.

options.text: Because they lack nucleic acid
options.explanation: Every virus carries DNA or RNA.

options.text: Because they perform none of the eight life processes on their own
options.explanation: The note gives exactly this reason.

options.text: Because they are too small to see with a microscope
options.explanation: Smallness is not the exclusion reason.

questions.stem: Which statement about virus reproduction is correct?

options.text: Viruses reproduce freely in soil and water
options.explanation: They need living cells.

options.text: Viruses reproduce by cell division
options.explanation: Viruses have no cells to divide.

options.text: Viruses never reproduce at all
options.explanation: They reproduce via host cells.

options.text: Viruses can reproduce only inside living host cells
options.explanation: Parasitic reproduction inside living cells is the named rule.

questions.stem: A tobacco plant shows a mosaic pattern of leaf discolouration and poor growth. Which pathogen fits, and what is the mechanism?

options.text: Tobacco mosaic virus, which damages chloroplast formation and so reduces photosynthesis
options.explanation: The note ties the discolouration to chloroplast damage and the poor growth to reduced photosynthesis.

options.text: Plasmodium falciparum, which destroys red blood cells
options.explanation: That is the malaria protoctist of humans.

options.text: Pneumococcus, which infects the lungs
options.explanation: That is a human lung pathogen.

options.text: A Mucor fungus, which rots the roots
options.explanation: The mosaic pattern is TMV's signature.

questions.stem: Which description of HIV's course through the immune system matches the note?

options.text: It is spread only through the air
options.explanation: The named routes are sexual contact and bodily-fluid exchange.

options.text: It begins flu-like, hides in the immune system for years, and can end in AIDS
options.explanation: The three-stage course is the note's account.

options.text: It kills within days of infection
options.explanation: The note describes years of hidden presence.

options.text: It never damages the immune system
options.explanation: Immune damage is its defining effect.

questions.stem: State the two components that make up every virus particle.
questions.modelAnswer: A protein coat and one type of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).

questions.stem: Name the virus that causes flu in humans.
Explain why a virus needs a host cell even though it carries its own genetic instructions.
questions.modelAnswer: A virus owns instructions but no machinery: with no cytoplasm, organelles or metabolism, it cannot run the eight life processes alone, so it must take over a host cell's metabolic equipment to build new virus particles.

questions.stem: A lab notebook lists three isolates: one taken from diseased tobacco leaves, one from a patient's immune cells, and one from an airway lining sample. Assign the likely virus to each sample.
questions.modelAnswer: Leaf isolate: tobacco mosaic virus; immune-cell isolate: HIV; airway lining isolate: influenza virus — each virus matches the tissue its disease targets.
